title: Holocene extinction

definition.text: The ongoing wave of extinctions of plants and animals, on land and at sea, caused by human activity in the current geological epoch.

facts.text: It is sometimes called the sixth extinction, and when the stress falls on human causes it is also called the Anthropocene extinction.
Species are now estimated to be disappearing 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background extinction rate.

Its drivers include climate change, destruction of wetlands, deforestation, overfishing, ocean acidification, population growth, economic growth and rising consumption, especially in affluent societies.
Scientists broadly agree that habitat destruction, resource consumption and the elimination of species are the main human drivers of the crisis.
The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment estimated that about one million species are at risk of extinction within decades because of human activities.
A 2023 study counted at least 73 animal genera lost since 1500, a rate it judged 35 times higher than the background rate without human impacts.
Population growth, economic growth and growth in consumption per person over the past two centuries are regarded as its underlying causes.
Proposed remedies include shifting economic activity toward low-impact sectors, plant-based diets, and enlarging protected areas on land and sea.

related: Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

title: Sixth mass extinction debate

definition.text: The scientific argument over whether today's human-caused extinctions already amount to a mass extinction like the five great ones in the fossil record.

facts.text: A mass extinction is defined as the loss of at least 75% of species within a geologically short period of less than 2 million years.
Some researchers call recent losses dramatic and serious but not yet a mass extinction in the palaeontological sense of the Big Five.
Others, including a 2022 review in Biological Reviews, argue that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is already under way.
Estimates of species lost per year range widely, from 1.5 to 40,000, but all point to human activity as the cause.

contested_note: Scientists disagree on whether current extinction rates already qualify as a mass extinction or only threaten one.

title: Human role in megafaunal extinctions

definition.text: The question of how far hunting by spreading human populations, rather than a changing climate, caused large animals to die out at the end of the last ice age.

facts.text: Megafaunal extinctions correlate with the arrival of humans, and human activity has been the main cause of mammal extinctions since the Late Pleistocene.
Worldwide, 178 species of the largest mammals died out between 52,000 and 9,000 BC.
A rival theory holds that climate change near the end of the Pleistocene stressed megafauna to extinction; some scientists think hunting and climate acted together.
Africa lost the fewest megafauna, possibly because its animals evolved alongside humans and learned to fear them.

contested_note: Sources disagree on how much human hunting, versus climate change, drove prehistoric megafaunal extinctions.

definition.text: The global crash of frog and salamander populations, driven partly by a fungal disease spread by human travel and the wildlife trade.

facts.text: Chytridiomycosis has caused severe declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions.
Amphibians are now the most endangered vertebrate group, though they survived three earlier mass extinctions over more than 300 million years.
Amphibian decline is treated as an indicator of environmental degradation.

definition.text: A species introduced by people to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered.

facts.text: Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity.
Invasions happen naturally, but human-assisted introductions have greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range.
Biological invasion is one of the five top drivers of global biodiversity loss and is growing with tourism and globalization.
Common traits of invaders include fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and earlier successful invasions.
An introduced species usually has to persist at low densities first, sometimes needing several introductions before it establishes.
Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative, though some can provide habitat or food for other organisms.
The term "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

title: Economic costs of invasive species

definition.text: The money lost to damage from invasive species and spent on controlling them.

facts.text: The economic impact of invasive species was estimated to exceed $423 billion a year as of 2019.
This cost has quadrupled every decade since 1970.
Costs split into direct production losses in farming and forestry and the costs of management.
Counting only lost production and management understates the cost; valuing lost species and ecosystem services would raise it sharply.
Estimated damage and control costs in the United States exceed $138 billion a year.
In France, damage costs were nearly eight times higher than spending on management.
Invasive trees can bring benefits such as commercial forestry, but returns from invasive species are usually far smaller than their costs.
Early detection and rapid response is often called the key to management, but it helps only when reintroduction is rare and response is affordable.

notes: S:0243ea2eff9a gives global management expenditures of about $1.4 trillion a year, far above the $423 billion impact estimate in S:ea4de4ef05ec; the two figures measure different things or one may be wrong, so check before using either alongside the other.

definition.text: The routes, mostly human, by which non-native species are carried to new places.

facts.text: Humans carry organisms faster and farther than natural range expansion, both deliberately and by accident.
Repeated traffic, such as ships between ports, creates recurring chances for arrival and establishment, called high propagule pressure.
A 2008 study found shipping, through hull fouling and ballast water, to be the dominant pathway for marine invasive species.
Deliberate biocontrol introductions can backfire: about 100 cane toads brought to Australia have become over 200 million.

definition.text: Inspection and quarantine rules on traded goods and ships that aim to stop pests and invasive species crossing borders.

facts.text: The first global standards, including the WTO's Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreement, were agreed in 1994 to block agricultural pests while allowing farm exports.
The International Maritime Organization oversees the Ballast Water Management Convention.
The Convention on Biological Diversity is the most significant international agreement on invasive species, but most of its measures are voluntary and unspecific.

definition.text: Ecological restoration applied to islands, chiefly by removing introduced species and bringing back native ones.

facts.text: Islands hold many of the world's endemic species but are very vulnerable to introduced species because of their small size.
A 2019 study found that eradicating invasive animals on just 169 islands would improve survival prospects for 9.4% of the most highly threatened island vertebrates.

definition.text: Introducing a non-native species on purpose to fill an ecological role left empty by an extinct native species.

facts.text: On islets off Mauritius, Aldabra giant tortoises introduced in 2000 and 2007 are replacing extinct native tortoises as seed dispersers and grazers of invasive plants.

definition.text: A standardized questionnaire that scores how likely a plant is to cause harm in a new environment, before it is introduced.

facts.text: Predicting plant impacts is especially useful because most plant introductions are intentional.
The total score is tied to a management action such as "prevent introduction".

definition.text: A genetic-engineering technique that makes a chosen gene spread through a population faster than normal inheritance, proposed for wiping out invasive animals.

facts.text: It has been proposed as a way to eliminate invasive mammals in New Zealand.
Normally offspring have a 50:50 chance of inheriting either version of a gene; a gene drive suppresses the unwanted version.

title: Critiques of the invasive species concept
article: Invasive species#Criticisms of the invasive species discourse

definition.text: Arguments that not all biological invasions are harmful and that the language of invasion misleads.

facts.text: An "effective invasion" is one where an alien species fills a vacant niche and joins local food webs without displacing natives.
Some scientists urge that species moving to escape a warming climate be treated as refugees rather than invaders.
Entomologist Chris D. Thomas argues most introduced species are neutral or beneficial, a minority view.

contested_note: A minority of scientists dispute the consensus that invasive species are mainly harmful and object to the term itself.

definition.text: The decline of living variety, either when species vanish from Earth entirely or when they decrease or disappear from a particular area.

facts.text: The loss is temporary if the damage can be reversed, for example through ecological restoration, and permanent if it cannot.
The current rate of global biodiversity loss is estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background extinction rate.
All contemporary biodiversity loss has been attributed to human activities.
Habitat destruction, often for farming, is currently a bigger driver of loss than climate change.
To measure loss at a site, scientists record its species richness and how it changes over time.
The WWF reported an average 68% population decline between 1970 and 2016 across 4,400 animal species and nearly 21,000 monitored populations.
Damaged ecosystems provide poorer ecosystem services, such as crop pollination, cleaning air and water, decomposing waste and forest products.
Of the 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets set in 2010, only six were partially achieved by 2020.

definition.text: The main human pressures behind today's loss of biodiversity: habitat loss, land-use intensification, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change.

facts.text: Edward O. Wilson coined the acronym HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human over-Population and Over-harvesting.
Jared Diamond describes an "Evil Quartet" of habitat destruction, overkill, introduced species and secondary extinctions.
Habitat destruction is the leading cause of biodiversity loss and species extinction worldwide.
A 2019 IPBES report found overfishing to be the main driver of mass species extinction in the oceans.
A 2021 IPBES and IPCC report found that biodiversity loss and climate change must be tackled together because they are inextricably linked.
Invasive species can drive natives extinct through competitive exclusion, niche displacement or hybridisation.

title: Agriculture as a driver of biodiversity loss

definition.text: The way expanding and intensifying farmland converts and degrades natural habitat, making agriculture the largest single cause of biodiversity decline on land.

facts.text: The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment found industrial agriculture to be the primary driver of biodiversity collapse.
The UN's Global Biodiversity Outlook 2014 estimated that 70% of projected terrestrial biodiversity loss is caused by agriculture.
As of 2023 about 38% of Earth's land surface was used for agriculture, the dominant land use.
Livestock systems occupy about 77% of agricultural land but provide less than 20% of the world's calories.
More than 17,000 species risk losing habitat by 2050 as farming expands to meet food needs.
A global shift toward mostly plant-based diets would free land for restoring ecosystems and biodiversity.

title: Population versus consumption debate

definition.text: The argument over whether human population growth or the scale and distribution of consumption is the deeper cause of biodiversity loss.

facts.text: Many scientists and the IPBES Global Assessment name population growth and overconsumption as the main underlying drivers.
Critics say habitat loss comes mainly from growth in export commodities such as soybean and oil palm, much of it for livestock feed or biofuel in richer economies.
A country's GDP correlates strongly with its environmental footprint, while its population size correlates negatively with footprint per person.

contested_note: Scholars disagree on whether population size or wealth-driven consumption is the main driver of biodiversity loss.

definition.text: The long fall in the total mass of wild mammals over the past 50,000 years while humans and livestock multiplied.

facts.text: The biomass of wild land mammals is believed to be seven times lower than prehistoric levels, and marine mammal biomass has fallen fivefold.
Of today's mammal biomass, only 4% is wild mammals, against 60% livestock and 36% humans.

definition.text: The especially fast loss of species living in rivers, lakes, swamps and deltas.

facts.text: Freshwater ecosystems cover 1% of Earth's surface but are home to about one third of vertebrate species.
Freshwater species are declining at twice the rate of land or ocean species.
Populations of migratory freshwater fish fell by 76% since 1970, and about one in three freshwater fish species is threatened with extinction.

definition.text: The process by which a natural habitat becomes unable to support the species that live there, so they move away or die.

facts.text: It is the leading cause of biodiversity loss and species extinction worldwide.
People cause it through resource use, agriculture, industry, urban sprawl, mining, logging and trawling.
Degradation, fragmentation and pollution can collapse a habitat without outright destroying it.
Of about 16 million square kilometres of original tropical rainforest, less than 9 million remain.
When habitat is destroyed, the carrying capacity for native species falls and populations decline, sometimes to extinction.
Endemic species with small ranges suffer most because they live nowhere else.
Its most profound impact on people is the loss of valuable ecosystem services such as climate regulation, pollination and water management.
Poor people suffer most, because wealthier people and countries can pay to keep receiving more than their share of natural resources.

definition.text: What people give up when a habitat is destroyed: the value the land would have produced if left natural.

facts.text: Converting forest to row crops can raise a country's food supply, yet the same land may be worth more supplying clean water, timber, ecotourism, or flood and drought control.

title: Proximate and underlying causes of deforestation

definition.text: The distinction between the direct activities that clear forest and the deeper demographic, economic and political forces behind them.

facts.text: Geist and Lambin (2002) reviewed 152 case studies of tropical forest loss.
The proximate causes clustered as agricultural expansion (96%), infrastructure expansion (72%) and wood extraction (67%).
Road and transport extension was the largest single proximate factor, and shifting cultivation was not the main cause in every region.
Most cases combine three to four underlying causes driving two to three proximate ones, so no single universal policy can control tropical deforestation.

title: Habitat fragmentation

definition.text: The breaking up of a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches, which splits populations and degrades ecosystems.

facts.text: It covers five changes: less total habitat, a lower interior-to-edge ratio, isolated fragments, one patch split into several, and smaller average patches.
People cause it by clearing native vegetation for agriculture, rural development, cities and hydroelectric reservoirs.
Fragmentation consistently reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75% and impairs ecosystem functions such as biomass production and nutrient cycling.
As a rough rule, keeping 10% of a habitat as a contiguous remnant results in a 50% loss of biodiversity.
Small, isolated populations can be wiped out by minor swings in climate or resources that large populations would absorb.
Dams and water diversions fragment aquatic habitats.
Its effects keep emerging for decades; experiments show biodiversity and ecosystem functioning still declining 20 or more years later.
Linking fragments with corridors of native vegetation, bridges or underpasses can ease isolation but does not restore interior habitat.

notes: Likely also drafted in a biodiversity chapter; fold at merge.

definition.text: The changed conditions along the border of a habitat fragment, where light, temperature and wind differ from the interior and favour different species.

facts.text: Fragmentation creates edge effects, and fires become more likely at edges as humidity drops and temperature and wind rise.
Exotic and pest species establish easily in disturbed edges.
Small fragments are poor for species that need interior habitat.
About 70% of the world's remaining forest lies within one kilometre of a forest edge.

title: SLOSS debate

definition.text: The argument over whether a single large reserve or several small ones of the same total area better conserves biodiversity in a fragmented landscape.

facts.text: The debate ran in ecology and conservation biology during the 1970s and 1980s.
A review of 381 significant effects of fragmentation per se found 76% positive and 24% negative, implying several small patches can sometimes beat one large one.
Many small forest islands typically cannot hold the biodiversity of one contiguous forest, even with greater combined area.
Where fragmentation per se has positive effects, land-sharing strategies could help species more than land-sparing ones.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether fragmentation itself, apart from habitat loss, harms or helps species, and so on whether large or many small reserves are better.

definition.text: The way immigrants from nearby populations keep small, isolated populations from dying out and recolonize patches where a species was lost.

facts.text: It was first described by Brown and Kodric-Brown and is widely used in metapopulation dynamics.
In fragmented landscapes the distance between fragments may stop a declining population being rescued by immigration.

definition.text: The loss of genetic variety, inbreeding and random genetic drift that threaten small populations left in habitat fragments.

facts.text: Remnant populations often hold only part of the genetic diversity of the former continuous habitat.
Fragmentation reduces gene flow and migration between populations.
Genetic drift, random change in a population's genetic makeup, matters more the smaller the population.
Inbreeding lowers reproduction and survival and adds to extinction risk in endangered species.

definition.text: Habitat fragmentation in which forests are reduced to small, isolated patches separated by farmland, open land or development.

facts.text: It is one of the greatest threats to forest biodiversity, especially in the tropics.
Remnant woodlands behave like islands of forest in a sea of fields and suburbs, following the principles of island biogeography.
Smaller or more isolated patches lose species faster than larger or better-connected ones.

definition.text: The global, local or functional loss of animal populations or species from ecological communities.

facts.text: Unlike extinction, it counts declines in animal numbers as well as disappearing species.
Population growth and better harvesting technology have stripped large vertebrates from many communities.
More than 50 percent of all wildlife is estimated to have been lost in the last 40 years.
Large mammals are especially vulnerable because they need large home ranges.
Over 50% of extinct animal species with a known cause were affected by invasive species.
Tropical regions such as the Brazilian Amazon, the Congo Basin and Indonesia are hit hardest.
Terrestrial mammal food-web links have fallen by 53% over the past 130,000 years as humans expanded.
It can weaken services such as nutrient cycling, decomposition, crop pollination, pest control and water quality.

definition.text: A forest whose habitat still looks intact but has lost its large mammals to human impact.

facts.text: The term comes from Kent H. Redford's 1992 article "The Empty Forest".
Hunted-out species may survive in small numbers yet be ecologically extinct, no longer playing their role.
Moderate hunting cuts mammalian game biomass by 80.7%, and heavy hunting by up to 93.7%.
Losing large seed dispersers and predators changes which trees regenerate and how prey species are spread.

definition.text: The loss of animal populations from the oceans, mostly through overexploitation.

facts.text: It has come later and less intensely than on land, with few marine extinctions but many local, ecological and commercial ones.
Overfishing has cut populations of oceanic sharks and rays by 71% since 1970.
The key services threatened are food supply and coastal storm protection.

definition.text: The clearing of a forest or stand of trees so the land can be put to a non-forest use such as farms, ranches or towns.

facts.text: Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half of that loss in the last century.
Between 2015 and 2020 deforestation ran at an estimated 10 million hectares a year, down from 16 million a year in the 1990s.
Agriculture is by far the main direct cause, with cropland expansion and pasture driving nearly 90% of global deforestation in 2025.
Logging, urbanization, mining and climate-driven wildfires are further drivers.
It destroys habitat and so causes biodiversity loss, extinctions, local climate change and displacement of forest peoples.
It reduces carbon uptake by forests, weakening their role in mitigating climate change.
Deforested regions often also suffer desertification and soil erosion.
Economic losses from deforestation in Brazil could reach around 317 billion dollars a year, about 7 times the value of the commodities it produces.

definition.text: The distinction between gross forest loss and net change, which subtracts new forest gained from forest lost over a period.

facts.text: Deforestation is the conversion of forest to other land uses, whether or not people caused it.
Net change can be positive or negative depending on whether gains exceed losses.
Reforestation and afforestation, especially in East Asia, are increasing forest area, which grew in 22 of the 50 most forested nations.

title: Drivers of deforestation

definition.text: The activities and forces that lead people to clear forests, chiefly farming and ranching, but also logging, mining, roads and wider economic pressures.

facts.text: Agricultural expansion remains the main driver of deforestation, forest fragmentation and forest biodiversity loss.
One breakdown attributes 48% of deforestation to subsistence farming, 32% to commercial agriculture, 14% to logging and 5% to fuel wood.
Beef is the primary driver in the Amazon, where around 80% of converted land is used to rear cattle.
By the 1990s most deforestation came from industrial factors such as extractive industries, large-scale ranching and extensive agriculture rather than subsistence activity.
Since 2001, commodity-driven deforestation, which is more likely to be permanent, has made up about a quarter of all forest disturbance.
About 90% of deforestation in most of the Amazon has occurred within 100 km of roads.
The role of population growth is contested: one study found high fertility a primary driver in only 8% of tropical cases.

related: Proximate and underlying causes of deforestation
Agriculture as a driver of biodiversity loss
contested_note: Sources disagree on how much population growth, as opposed to commodity demand and economic conditions, drives deforestation.

definition.text: The economic reason forests are over-cleared: many of their benefits are sold in no market, so owners see more profit in converting them than in keeping them.

facts.text: Many important forest functions have no markets and hence no economic value readily apparent to forest owners or dependent communities.
Short-term gains from converting forest or overharvesting wood typically lose long-term income and biological productivity.
Poverty and agricultural rent were found to be principal factors leading to deforestation.
Proposed policies would align economic activity in critical forests with their value for ecosystem services and climate mitigation, using tools such as certification, eco-tariffs and traceability.

definition.text: Handing legal rights over forest land to the Indigenous peoples and communities who live there, as a way to slow deforestation.

facts.text: Transferring land from public ownership to Indigenous inhabitants is argued to be a cost-effective way to conserve forests.
In Brazil, forests under Indigenous tenure are cleared at even lower rates than national parks.
Community concessions in Congolian rainforests show much less deforestation, as communities have reason to manage land sustainably.

definition.text: The link between clearing forests and the spread of diseases that jump from animals to people.

facts.text: Forest-associated diseases include malaria, Chagas disease, sleeping sickness, leishmaniasis, Lyme disease, HIV and Ebola.
Most new human infectious diseases, including SARS-CoV-2, are zoonotic, and their emergence may be tied to forest loss and human expansion into forests.
Forest clearance for pig farms in Malaysia increased the spread of Nipah virus.

definition.text: The popular but mistaken belief that rainforests supply much of the world's oxygen.

facts.text: Rainforests add little net oxygen to the atmosphere, so deforestation barely changes oxygen levels.
About 50 percent of Earth's oxygen is produced by algae, mostly in the oceans.

definition.text: The process by which land becomes less healthy and productive through human activity or natural conditions.

facts.text: Unsustainable land management is often the main cause.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005 defined it as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of drylands.
The UN estimates about 30% of land is degraded worldwide, with about 3.2 billion people living in degrading areas.
Around 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded every year.
Over 60% of human-induced land degradation occurs on agricultural land.
It lowers crop yields and ecosystem diversity, raises vulnerability to floods and droughts, and releases greenhouse gases.
Degraded land is less resilient, so further shocks can drive still more degradation.
Reversing 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year.

definition.text: The way heavy use of fertilizers and other inputs hides falling soil productivity on intensive farms while worsening the underlying damage.

facts.text: Farmers decide mainly on productivity and profit, so degradation on farms reflects local choices and global drivers such as trade and climate change.
Compensating with inputs keeps yields high in the short term but brings diminishing returns, higher costs, acidification and pollution.
Threshold effects can eventually lead to land abandonment in long-farmed areas.

title: Land degradation neutrality

definition.text: The UN goal of a world where degraded land and soil are restored and land degradation no longer advances, set under Sustainable Development Goal 15.

facts.text: UN Sustainable Development Goal Target 15.3 aims by 2030 to combat desertification, restore degraded land and soil, and strive for a land degradation-neutral world.
Restoring degraded land yields ecosystem services that benefit society at large, making it a collective-action problem for providing public goods.
The UNCCD pursues LDN through its 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, along with fighting desertification, land degradation and drought.
The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration lists the UNCCD's LDN target among the agreements restoration helps achieve.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own. Verification: check the 2009 date in S:8e427fdb5c28 against its source.

definition.text: Harvesting a renewable resource, such as fish, forests, groundwater or wildlife, faster than it can replenish, to the point of diminishing returns.

facts.text: Ecologists count it among the five main activities threatening global biodiversity.
A population is overexploited when harvested at a rate its natural mortality and reproduction cannot sustain, which can wipe out populations or whole species.
Harvesting can be sustainable if it stays within limits, as in well-managed fisheries.
An aquifer is overexploited when water is extracted faster than it recharges; it is then said to be overdrafted.
Forests are overexploited when logging outpaces reforestation.
It threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates, and has affected about 40% of the bird species extinct since 1500.
Excluding edible fish, the illegal wildlife trade is valued at $10 billion a year.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons explains how people sharing a resource, each acting in self-interest, can overexploit and destroy it.

definition.text: The crash of a fished population, conventionally when its biomass falls by more than 95 percent of the highest level recorded.

facts.text: Pushing harvests past the maximum sustainable yield, usually reached near 30% of pre-harvest biomass, leads to collapse.
Atlantic cod collapsed abruptly in 1992 after heavy exploitation and failed to recover even after fishing stopped.
About 25% of world fisheries are overexploited below the biomass that maximizes sustainable yield.
A 2008 study found strong evidence that individual transferable quotas help prevent collapses and restore declining fisheries.

definition.text: Knock-on effects through a food web when overharvesting removes a key species, especially a top predator.

facts.text: Losing a top predator lets its prey multiply and overexploit their own food, sometimes until they too collapse.
Hunting of sea otters released sea urchins, which stripped kelp into urchin barrens and caused secondary extinctions.
After a 1911 treaty protected the last 32 sea otters in one group, they multiplied and the depleted areas slowly recovered.

definition.text: The two-way link in which clearing forests warms the climate and a changing climate in turn damages forests.

facts.text: Land use change, mainly deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels.
Emissions come from burning forest biomass and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon.
As of 2019 deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
The relationship is an amplifying feedback: more tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms and more tree loss.
Standing tropical forests help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C.
In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and forest ecosystem collapse.

title: Deforestation and rainfall
article: Deforestation and climate change#Changes in rainfall

definition.text: The drying effect of forest loss: fewer trees release less water vapour, so less rain falls nearby.

facts.text: Reduced rainfall brings a hotter, drier climate, longer dry seasons, more fires and disrupted pollination.
A 2025 study estimated deforestation caused about 74% of the decline in dry-season rainfall across the Brazilian Legal Amazon from 1985 to 2020.
Deforestation in the Congo is expected to cut regional rainfall by up to 8-10% by 2100.

definition.text: The change in how much sunlight a cleared landscape reflects, which alters warming beyond the effect of released carbon.

facts.text: Studies since the early 1990s show large-scale deforestation north of 50°N gives net global cooling, while tropical deforestation produces substantial warming.
Carbon-only metrics miss this because bare high-latitude ground is much more reflective than intact forest.

definition.text: How well represented a species is in a particular ecosystem, usually counted as individuals per sample.

facts.text: Relative species abundance compares one species' abundance with that of others in the ecosystem; both measures feed into biodiversity calculations.
Large animals are counted with methods such as spotlight, track and roadkill counts; plants are often measured by the share of a plot they cover.
In most ecosystems a few species are abundant and many are rare; abundant species tend to be generalists and rare ones specialists.
Abundant species produce more colonizing offspring, a feedback that yields widespread core species and scarce satellite species.

definition.text: A description of how common or rare each species is within an ecosystem.

facts.text: It is one of the most basic and widely used measurements in ecology, with many methods of analysis.
Distributions are usually skewed so that a few species make up most of the individuals collected.

definition.text: A quick field rating that scores a species in a plot as Dominant, Abundant, Frequent, Occasional or Rare.

facts.text: DAFOR and ACFOR are semi-quantitative ratings based on viewing an area of set size.
They give rough estimates but are not exact or objective, so better methods should be used where available.

definition.text: The part of biodiversity that matters for farming: the variety of plants, animals and microbes, at gene, species and ecosystem levels, that sustains food and farm production.

facts.text: It is managed by farmers, pastoralists, fishers and forest dwellers and gives rural livelihoods stability, adaptability and resilience.
It supports food, nutrition and livelihood security and is critical for climate adaptation and mitigation.
About 6,000 species are commonly used for food, by a conservative estimate.
75% of the 115 major crop species grown worldwide rely on pollinators.
It is threatened by urbanization, deforestation, monocultures, abandonment of traditional practices and Westernized diets.
Its loss leads to genetic erosion, including the loss of locally adapted landraces and breeds.
Agrobiodiversity provides income through food and raw materials and by supporting services such as pollination, pest control and nutrient cycling.

definition.text: The decline in the number of crop species grown and in the genetic variety within each crop.

facts.text: Over the past 50 years both genetic diversity within crops and the number of species commonly grown have fallen sharply.
It threatens food security because people depend on ever fewer varieties of ever fewer crops.
The Irish potato blight of 1846, which contributed to one million deaths, struck because only two vulnerable potato varieties were planted.
When rice grassy stunt virus spread in the 1970s, only one of 6,273 varieties tested was resistant.

definition.text: Conserving species or genetic material away from their natural habitat, in places such as seed banks, genebanks, botanical gardens and cryobanks.

facts.text: It is considered a fairly reliable way to keep genetic diversity over the long term because stored material changes little.
Over 7 million samples are held in 1,750 genebanks worldwide.
In situ conservation, by contrast, lets species keep evolving in response to natural and human pressures; practitioners recommend combining both.

definition.text: The genetic variety of bird and mammal species, breeds and populations used for food and farming.

facts.text: About 8,800 breeds of birds and mammals within 38 species are used for food and agriculture.
This diversity can be held in live animals or in stored material such as frozen semen or embryos.

definition.text: The average species diversity found within individual sites at a local scale.

facts.text: R. H. Whittaker introduced it together with beta and gamma diversity.
Whittaker's idea was that a landscape's total diversity (gamma) depends on local diversity (alpha) and on how much sites differ (beta).
No consensus exists on the right spatial scale, so it can be measured for subunits of any size.
Researchers often measure it with species richness, the Shannon index or the Simpson index.

title: Effective number of species
article: Diversity index#Effective number of species or Hill numbers

definition.text: The number of equally common species that would give the same average species abundance as the real, uneven community.

facts.text: It has been proposed as a universal measure of species diversity because it is easier to grasp than diversity indices.
Its values for different orders q are called Hill numbers; the order sets how much weight rare versus abundant species get.
At q = 0 it equals species richness; larger q gives more weight to the most abundant species and a smaller diversity value.
Most common diversity indices are simple transformations of it.

definition.text: The normal rate at which species go extinct through Earth's history, outside mass extinction events.

facts.text: Extinction is a normal part of evolution, and the background rate measures how often it happens naturally.
It is the yardstick for showing how much faster species are vanishing today.
It is roughly one extinction per million species-years; at that rate one bird species would go extinct about every 400 years.
Under normal rates species typically last 5–10 million years; mammal species average about 1 million years.
Background rates have fallen over the Phanerozoic, which has been linked to increasing ocean oxygenation.

title: Beta diversity

definition.text: A measure of how much species composition differs between sites, defined as the ratio of regional to local species diversity.

facts.text: Whittaker introduced it alongside alpha and gamma diversity.
Whittaker's form says how many completely distinct subunits there would be if total and average diversity stayed the same but no species were shared.
Many types now exist, including absolute, Whittaker's and proportional species turnover.
Studies disagree on patterns: in Borneo, moths showed higher beta diversity in primary forest but trees showed it in logged forest.
Invasive species appear to raise local diversity while lowering beta diversity.

contested_note: Studies reach conflicting conclusions about beta-diversity patterns, likely because they use different spatial scales.

definition.text: Formulas that express beta diversity as the amount by which a whole dataset's diversity exceeds that of an average site.

facts.text: Additive partitioning gives absolute species turnover; dividing it by alpha diversity gives Whittaker's species turnover.
For two sites with presence-absence data, Whittaker's turnover equals one minus the Sørensen similarity index.
Dividing absolute turnover by gamma diversity gives proportional turnover, equal for two sites to one minus the Jaccard index.

definition.text: A region with exceptionally high biodiversity, especially species found nowhere else, that is threatened by human activity.

facts.text: Norman Myers developed the concept in articles in 1988 and 1990, revised in 2000.
To qualify, a region must hold at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (over 0.5% of the world total) and have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation.
Globally, 36 zones qualify.
Hotspots cover just 2.4% of the planet's surface yet support nearly 60% of the world's plant, bird, mammal, reptile and amphibian species.
Most hotspots are tropical, and only a small share of their land is protected.
Critics note that the hotspot approach ignores the cost of conservation and phylogenetic diversity.

definition.text: Systems that rank places for conservation by their species richness, endemism and threat, so limited funds go where they matter most.

facts.text: WWF's Global 200 Ecoregions picks priorities from 14 terrestrial, 3 freshwater and 4 marine habitat types, and every hotspot contains at least one.
BirdLife International has identified 218 Endemic Bird Areas and more than 11,000 Important Bird Areas.
The Alliance for Zero Extinction has identified 595 sites holding the most threatened endemic species.

definition.text: The process by which separate ecological communities become more and more alike over time.

facts.text: It can be genetic, taxonomic or functional, and it means a loss of beta diversity.
It stems mainly from extinctions of native species and invasions of non-native ones, and human pressure has accelerated it.
It need not lower local species richness; communities can gain species and still grow more similar.
In 201 Chilean watersheds compared over 200 years, about 65% of comparisons showed homogenization.
Ecologists worry that simpler, more similar ecosystems will be less resilient to stress.

definition.text: Meat from wild animals hunted for people to eat, especially in Africa.

facts.text: It is a main source of animal protein and income for poor rural communities in humid tropical forests.
As of 2016, 301 terrestrial mammal species were threatened with extinction by bushmeat hunting, including all pangolin species.
The trade in West and Central Africa was estimated at 1–5 million tonnes a year around the turn of the 21st century.
Hunting for one's own use in large landscapes can be sustainable, but market hunting threatens large, slow-breeding species.
The "bushmeat crisis", coined in 2007, names the double threat of vanishing food supplies and wildlife extinctions.
Logging roads and trucks give hunters access to remote forests and carry meat to towns.
Suggested remedies include affordable alternative protein, giving communities rights over wildlife, and enforcing protected areas.

definition.text: The link by which falling fish supplies push people to hunt more wild animals, because the two foods substitute for each other.

facts.text: In Ghana, depletion of fish stocks by foreign and local fleets led people to hunt animals in nature reserves instead.
Over 30 years of data tie sharp declines in 41 wildlife species to a falling fish supply.
A decline in one resource raises demand and price for the other.

definition.text: The jump of diseases from wild animals to people, made more likely by hunting, butchering and eating wildlife.

facts.text: HIV likely first passed to humans through contact with infected bushmeat.
Ebola outbreaks in the Congo Basin and Gabon in the 1990s were associated with butchering and eating chimpanzees and bonobos.
Deforestation, fragmentation and expanding human activity in wildlife habitat increase contact and so spillover.
The One Health framework treats human, animal and environmental health as interconnected.

definition.text: A rating of whether a species or other group still exists and how likely it is to go extinct in the near future.

facts.text: Assessments weigh population trends, breeding success and known threats, not just how many individuals remain.
The two international systems are run by the IUCN and by CITES; others work at regional, national and local levels.
The IUCN Red List is the best-known system, sorting species into nine groups using criteria such as rate of decline, population size, range and fragmentation.
In Red List usage, "threatened" groups three categories: critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable.
Other categories run from Extinct and Extinct in the Wild to Near Threatened, Least Concern and Data Deficient.
CITES, in force since 1975, aims to ensure that international trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival.
Seafood consumer guides rate species in a similar way but also weigh fishing impacts such as bycatch and bottom trawling.

definition.text: A wild plant closely related to a domesticated crop, such as its wild ancestor.

facts.text: Natural selection in the wild gives them useful traits that breeders can cross into crops, and modern varieties of most major crops carry genes from wild relatives.
Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov first recognized their importance in the early 20th century.
They are likely to be a critical resource for food security as climate change makes ecosystems less stable.
In 2016, 29% of wild relative species were missing entirely from the world's genebanks and 24% more had fewer than 10 samples.

title: Decline in insect populations

definition.text: The widespread fall in insect numbers across many insect groups, reported since the 2010s, sometimes extending to species extinction.

facts.text: Insects account for up to 90% of all animal species.
Estimates of insect species at risk of extinction range from 10% to 40%.
A 2020 meta-analysis of 166 long-term studies found land insects declining about 9% per decade, while freshwater insects rose 11% per decade.
Causes ranked by one study: habitat loss to intensive farming and cities, pollution from pesticides and fertilisers, pathogens and introduced species, then climate change.
A German study found a 76% seasonal decline in flying insect biomass in nature reserves over 1989–2016.
The decline threatens insect-eating birds and mammals and services such as crop pollination and waste disposal.
Global trends are hard to infer because data vary by time, place and species and are concentrated in Western Europe and North America.

related: Agriculture as a driver of biodiversity loss
contested_note: A 2019 review's projection that 40% of insect species could go extinct within decades was challenged, and global estimates remain uncertain.

title: Wildflower strips
article: Decline in insect populations#Wildflower strips and buffer zones

definition.text: Strips of land at field edges sown with pollinator-friendly flowering plants to support insects and farmland wildlife.

facts.text: They aim to sustain local biodiversity, conserve insects, restore farmland birds and offset the harms of agricultural intensification.
Pesticide-reduced buffer zones around nature reserves have also been proposed, after a German study found insects there carried about 16 pesticides on average.

title: Desertification

definition.text: The gradual degradation of fertile land in dry regions into desert, through natural processes and human activities.

facts.text: Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation, driven by drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees for fuel or building.
Bare dry soil blows or washes away, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan.
Drylands cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries.
Some 10–20% of drylands are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification.
Climate change is expected to expand drylands from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100.
Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain even when they benefit society and the environment.
Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks are used to fix soil and cut erosion.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

title: Desertification causes debate

definition.text: The dispute over how much local overgrazing and farming, rather than climate, drive desertification.

facts.text: Early studies blamed overgrazing by livestock as a leading cause.
Sahel drought is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall variability driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases.
Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions re-greened the Sahel, leading some scholars to call farming-induced vegetation loss a minor factor.
By 2005 there were more than 100 formal definitions of desertification.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether local overexploitation or climate variability is the main recent driver of desertification.

definition.text: A number that measures how many different types, usually species, a dataset or community contains, often weighted by how common each is.

facts.text: Indices summarize aspects of biodiversity such as richness, evenness and dominance, making communities or sites easy to compare.
Abundance can be measured as numbers of individuals, biomass or coverage.
Richness is a simple count of types and is popular in ecology because abundance data are often lacking.
The Shannon and Simpson indices also account for each type's proportional abundance.
The same measures are used outside ecology, for demographic groups or letters of the alphabet.

definition.text: A diversity index that measures the uncertainty in predicting the species of an individual picked at random from a community.

facts.text: Claude Shannon proposed the measure in 1948 to quantify entropy in strings of text.
The more types there are and the more evenly they are represented, the harder the prediction and the higher the value.
Log bases 2, 10 and e give values in bits, decits and nats respectively.
Its exponential is the effective number of species of order 1.

definition.text: A measure of concentration equal to the probability that two individuals picked at random belong to the same type.

facts.text: Edward H. Simpson introduced it in 1949 to measure concentration among types.
Economists know the same measure as the Herfindahl or Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI).
One minus the index, the Gini–Simpson index, is the probability that the two individuals are of different types.
Its inverse equals the effective number of species of order 2.

title: Ecological effects of biodiversity

definition.text: The ways the variety of species and genes in a community shapes how that community functions.

facts.text: Research has focused on how diversity relates to productivity and to community stability.
More diverse communities appear to produce more biomass and to be more stable when disturbed.
Productivity is usually measured as the total aboveground plant biomass in an area.
Many long-term grassland studies find that diversity enhances productivity, though results vary.
Diversity in species' functional roles may predict productivity better than the number of species.
If diversity stabilizes ecosystems, losing species could feed back into further losses.
Losing species also means losing potential foods, medicines, industrial products and tourism.
Habitat fragmentation alters biodiversity-ecosystem functioning relationships across scales, and losses of both can continue two decades after fragmentation.

contested_note: Experiments disagree on whether diversity itself or species composition drives productivity, and on whether diversity reduces invasion.
notes: This page is the concept the phrase dossier calls "Biodiversity and ecosystem functioning"; the phrase concept was folded here rather than drafted separately.

title: Diversity-productivity mechanisms
article: Ecological effects of biodiversity#Effects on community productivity

definition.text: The proposed reasons more diverse plant communities produce more biomass: complementarity, facilitation and the sampling effect.

facts.text: Complementarity: species with different resource needs together use resources more completely.
Facilitation: some species improve conditions for others, as nurse plants or nitrogen-fixing legumes do.
Sampling effect: a diverse plot is more likely to include a highly productive species, a composition effect rather than diversity itself.

title: Diversity-stability mechanisms
article: Ecological effects of biodiversity#Effects on community stability

definition.text: The proposed reasons species-rich communities vary less over time: averaging, negative covariance, insurance and resistance to invasion.

facts.text: Averaging effect: different species' responses average out, a statistical result of summing random variables.
Negative covariance: competing species do well when others do badly, lowering overall variance.
Insurance effect: more species means more chance of redundant stabilizers that respond to shocks in different ways.
Evidence that diversity resists invasion is mixed, with many studies finding the opposite.

contested_note: Findings on whether diversity improves resistance and resilience, unlike temporal stability, are contested.

definition.text: A species at very high risk of going extinct in the near future, worldwide or in a particular region.

facts.text: Species become endangered mainly through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation.
On the IUCN Red List, "Endangered" sits between "Vulnerable" and "Critically Endangered".
One IUCN criterion: a population that falls 20% within five years and has fewer than 2,500 mature individuals left.
Another: a population decline of 50% to 70% over 10 years or three generations, whichever is longer.
In 2026 the IUCN Red List named 49,500 species worldwide as threatened with extinction.
Many nations protect such species by banning hunting or harvest, restricting development or creating protected areas.
The US bald eagle recovered from 417 nesting pairs in 1963 to 71,400 by 2020 through habitat protection, legal protection and a DDT ban.

definition.text: Breeding rare or endangered species in controlled settings such as zoos and reserves to keep them from going extinct.

facts.text: Some of the oldest examples come from the menageries of European and Asian rulers, such as Père David's deer.
It is hard to apply to highly mobile species such as migratory cranes and fishes.
Too small a captive population risks inbreeding from a reduced gene pool.

definition.text: The idea that letting people legally own and profit from endangered animals can give them reasons to protect rather than poach them.

facts.text: Legal, for-profit private farming has substantially increased southern black and white rhinoceros populations.
Ecotourism and sales give owners strong economic incentives to look after rhinos rather than poach them.
Farming can backfire: turtle farmers may seek the last wild specimens as breeding stock.

title: Shifting recovery baselines
article: Endangered species#Conservation baselines and proposed paradigm shifts

definition.text: Redefining what counts as recovery for a species near extinction, as a last resort, to set more realistic goals.

facts.text: Options include moving a species to better habitat, letting it breed with similar species, or accepting a smaller stable population.
Florida panthers were saved by introducing Texas cougars, creating well-adapted panther–cougar hybrids.
It carries extra risks and is usually tried only after recovery within the natural range has failed.

title: Endemism

definition.text: The state of a species being found naturally in only one defined place, such as a single island, country or region.

facts.text: Conservation biology uses endemism to measure a place's biodiversity and to judge extinction risk.
Its opposite is a cosmopolitan distribution, a global or widespread range.
Endemics are not necessarily rare, and rare species are not necessarily endemic.
Isolation breeds endemism, so remote islands such as Hawaii, the Galápagos and Socotra hold many endemics.
Charles Darwin first used "endemic" for a species restricted to one place, in 1872.
Endemics are at greater risk than widespread species from habitat loss and fast climate change because their ranges are small.
Endemic species are used to find conservation priorities, an idea behind biodiversity hotspots, though some argue endemism does not track threat.

contested_note: Some scientists argue endemism is a poor measure of biodiversity or threat because high-endemism areas do not consistently match them.

definition.text: Two kinds of endemic species: relics of once-widespread groups now confined to a small area, and young species that have not yet spread beyond where they arose.

facts.text: Stebbins and Major introduced the terms in 1965 to describe California's endemics.
The ginkgo tree is an example of a paleoendemic species.
Phylogenetic endemism weights species by how evolutionarily distinct they are, not just how many are endemic.
How endemism is categorized affects how hotspots are defined and so where conservation money goes.

definition.text: Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies.

facts.text: A species can be functionally extinct before its last member dies, if the few survivors can no longer reproduce and recover.
More than 99.9% of all species that ever lived are extinct, and the average species lasts 1–10 million years.
Habitat degradation is currently the main human cause of extinctions, and agriculture is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide.
Humans have become an extra cause of extinction, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world.
Fossil studies confirm extinction caused by climate change; a 2003 review predicted 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change.
There have been at least five mass extinctions in the history of life on Earth.
A 2014 special edition of Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.
Because the moment of extinction is hard to pin down over a large range, it is usually decided after the fact.

definition.text: Coextinction is the loss of one species because another species it depends on has gone extinct.

facts.text: Parasitic insects can die out after their hosts are lost, and predators can vanish when their prey or a plant its pollinator disappears.
It is especially common when a keystone species goes extinct.

definition.text: Genetic pollution is uncontrolled interbreeding with introduced or hybrid populations that swamps a native species' gene pool.

facts.text: It most threatens rare species that come into contact with abundant ones, whose hybrids deplete the pure gene pool.
The endangered wild water buffalo is most threatened by genetic pollution from the abundant domestic water buffalo.
Such extinctions may not be visible from an animal's outward appearance.

definition.text: A Lazarus taxon is a species or group thought to be extinct that is later found again.

facts.text: The coelacanth was known only from fossils and thought extinct since the end of the Cretaceous, until a living one was found off South Africa in 1938.
Such reappearances show how hard it is to establish exactly when a species has gone extinct.

title: De-extinction by cloning

definition.text: De-extinction is the proposal to bring an extinct species back to life by cloning it from DNA in its remains.

facts.text: Proposed targets include the mammoth, the thylacine, the dodo and the Pyrenean ibex, which has been cloned before.
Success would need enough clones from the DNA of different individuals to form a viable population.
It seems possible in theory, though bioethical and philosophical objections have been raised.
IUCN guidelines from 2016 hold that an extinct species cannot be perfectly recreated, so the results are called 'proxy species'.
It could restore lost ecological functions but carries risks such as disease transmission, hybridization and animal suffering.

contested_note: Critics see de-extinction as 'playing God' and a threat to animal welfare, while others defend it as restoring nature.

definition.text: Extinction debt is the future extinction of species that has already been set in motion by past events such as habitat loss.

facts.text: It arises from time lags: long-lived trees, for example, may survive for years after new trees can no longer be produced.
Habitat fragmentation and habitat destruction are its best-known drivers, because they cut off species' ability to recolonize other patches.
It is most likely in long-lived species and in specialists with narrow habitat needs.
The term was first used in 1994 by Tilman, May, Lehman and Nowak; it is likened to the 'climate commitment' of warming that continues after emissions stop.
Modelling of species–area relationships suggests 80–90% of the extinctions due to past Amazon deforestation have yet to happen.
In the Azores, where over 95% of native forest was destroyed in 600 years, more than half of arthropods are thought committed to extinction.
It means protecting today's habitat may not be enough, but the long delay gives time for habitat restoration to prevent losses.

definition.text: Extinction debt is detected by checking whether today's species better match past habitat than present habitat, or by comparing cleared and intact areas.

facts.text: It is hard to measure because the processes are slow and noisy and tiny remnant populations are hard to count, so estimates are very uncertain.
The size of the debt can only be estimated if past species populations are known as well as present ones.
In moss microcosm experiments, insect species took 6–12 months to die out after habitat was destroyed.

title: Extinction event

definition.text: An extinction event, or mass extinction, is a widespread and rapid fall in the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It happens when extinctions outpace both the normal background extinction rate and the rate at which new species form.
Estimates of how many major mass extinctions occurred in the last 540 million years range from five to more than twenty.
The largest, the end-Permian 'Great Dying', killed about 81% of marine species and an estimated 70% of land vertebrate species.
Large extinctions tend to follow when a biosphere already under long-term stress suffers a short-term shock.
Research since 1982 concludes that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is under way, with extinctions over 1,000 times the background rate since 1900.
This sixth extinction is driven by population growth, economic growth and overconsumption of natural resources.
After a mass extinction, usually only adaptable 'weedy' species survive, and new groups can take over the emptied niches.

contested_note: Scientists still debate the causes of the mass extinctions.

title: Big Five mass extinctions
article: Extinction event#The "Big Five" mass extinction events

definition.text: The Big Five are the five geological intervals of exceptional diversity loss identified by Jack Sepkoski and David Raup in 1982.

facts.text: They are the Late Ordovician, Late Devonian, Permian–Triassic, Triassic–Jurassic and Cretaceous–Paleogene extinctions.
The Cretaceous–Paleogene event 66 million years ago removed about 75% of all species, including the non-avian dinosaurs.
They seem to be the largest of a fairly smooth continuum of extinction events rather than a clearly separate class.
A 2021 study linked the Big Five with about 5.2 °C of warming.

title: Extinction risk from climate change

definition.text: Climate change can drive species extinct by shifting temperature and weather outside the conditions each species has evolved to live in.

facts.text: Species facing changing conditions can either adapt where they are or move to a new habitat with suitable conditions.
So far few recorded extinctions are blamed on climate change: the IUCN links only 20 of 864 species extinctions to it, usually on weak evidence.
A 2011 review of 74 studies found they projected an average loss of 11.2% of species by 2100.
A 2018 study estimated that at 1.5 °C, 2 °C and 3.2 °C of warming, 6%, 18% and about 49% of insect species would lose over half their climatic range.
Updated 2022 estimates show only 0.2% of coral reefs could withstand marine heatwaves at 1.5 °C of warming, compared with 84% now.
Climate change already threatens 45% of at-risk marine species, though overfishing, the aquarium trade, urban development and pollution currently do more damage.
Loss of the species that supply food, fibre and energy hits nature-dependent communities' livelihoods, especially in Africa.
Prevention means limiting warming and protecting present and near-future habitat, as in the 30x30 effort.

contested_note: A 2021 estimate that warming like that of the Big Five would cause a similar mass extinction was disputed the next year.
notes: The 15–37% 'committed to extinction by 2050' estimate (S:e2f193dfc1a4) also appears on Extinction (S:0f5c19d8d726); both describe the same 2004 study.

title: Assisted migration
article: Extinction risk from climate change#Assisted migration

definition.text: Assisted migration means moving plants or animals to a new habitat so they can escape a climate their old range no longer offers.

facts.text: It is proposed for species that disperse poorly, have long generation times or small populations.
It can be passive, through wildlife corridors, or active transport, and it has already been used to save several North American tree species.
It is controversial because some moved species may become invasive in their new homes.

contested_note: Critics worry that relocated species may become invasive.

definition.text: A flagship species is a popular species chosen as a symbol to win public support and money for conserving nature in a place.

facts.text: The idea is essentially a marketing one; well-known examples include the Bengal tiger, giant panda, black rhinoceros and Asian elephant.
Flagships can skew conservation priorities toward charismatic species at the expense of more threatened, less appealing ones.
All ten of the most charismatic animal groups in a 2018 study are endangered, so charisma alone does not prevent extinction.
Flagships can clash with local people, as with the Asian elephant where human–elephant conflict occurs, a problem called 'flagship mutiny'.

definition.text: Gamma diversity is the total species diversity of a whole landscape.

facts.text: R. H. Whittaker introduced it together with alpha and beta diversity.
In Whittaker's view, landscape diversity (gamma) is set by the average diversity of local sites (alpha) and how much those sites differ (beta).
There is no agreed spatial scale for it, and a sample usually underestimates the true diversity of a larger area; a species–area curve can estimate the shortfall.

definition.text: Genetic diversity is the total variety of inherited characteristics within the genetic makeup of a species.

facts.text: It lets populations adapt to changing environments, because some individuals are more likely to carry variants suited to new conditions.
Lower genetic diversity makes a population more vulnerable to changes such as climate change or new diseases; koalas' low diversity is linked to their failure to fight off chlamydia.
Small populations lose diversity by chance (genetic drift) and through inbreeding, and a bottleneck can cut diversity rapidly.
A 2007 study found that diversity within species and diversity among species depend on each other.
Loss of genetic diversity in domestic animals has been attributed to the spread of markets and economic globalization.
Mutation and gene flow, such as pollen carried by wind or migrating birds, add new genetic variants to a population.

definition.text: Selective breeding has produced monocultures, whole farms of nearly genetically identical crop plants.

facts.text: With little genetic diversity, a disease that attacks one genetic variant can wipe out an entire crop.
Ireland's nineteenth-century Great Famine was caused partly by this: potatoes grown from pieces of one parent plant were effectively clones, open to epidemic.

definition.text: Genetic rescue is the attempt to make a struggling population more viable by adding genetic diversity to it.

facts.text: Eight Texas panthers were added to the declining, inbred Florida panther population, raising genetic variation and markedly boosting population growth.
Keeping genetic diversity high is an important part of species rescue efforts.

definition.text: Genetic diversity in a population is measured with simple indicators of how varied its genes are.

facts.text: Measures include the share of polymorphic loci in the genome, heterozygosity, alleles per locus and nucleotide diversity.
Simulation software uses allele frequencies and population size to predict a population's future.

definition.text: Genetic erosion is any decrease in genetic diversity, whether natural or caused by people.

facts.text: Each organism's genome is unique, so when one dies without breeding, any unique genes it carried are lost.
Habitat loss and fragmentation, often from farming and infrastructure, and already low diversity speed it up; small populations are most at risk.
Low genetic diversity brings inbreeding and weak immunity, which can 'fast-track' a species toward extinction.
In crops, the main driver is replacing local varieties of plants and animals with non-local ones, often commercial varieties.
Many researchers see modern agriculture's push toward genetic and ecological uniformity as the main problem in managing farm ecosystems.
Many bioscience safeguards are still too expensive, so protecting habitat and letting species live naturally in it remains the best defence.
Keeping at least 90% of the northern quoll's genetic diversity requires conserving at least eight populations across Australia.

title: Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
article: Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

definition.text: The Global Assessment Report is the IPBES report on the global state of biodiversity, whose summary for policymakers came out on 6 May 2019.

facts.text: It reviews 50 years of change, drawing on over 15,000 scientific publications and Indigenous knowledge; it is the first UN global biodiversity assessment since the 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.
Of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species, 1 million are threatened with extinction, including 40% of amphibians and more than a third of marine mammals.
It ranks the drivers: changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive alien species.
Wild mammal biomass has fallen by 82%, while humans and their farm animals now make up 96% of all mammal biomass.
Over 50 years the human population doubled and GDP per person quadrupled while biodiversity declined catastrophically.
Pollinator loss threatens food production worth $235 to $577 billion a year, and coastal losses threaten up to 300 million people's livelihoods.
It urged countries not to fixate on economic growth, to cut subsidies to industries harmful to nature and to fund beneficial programmes instead.

title: Global biodiversity

definition.text: Global biodiversity is the total variety of life forms on Earth.

facts.text: Estimates of the number of species alive today run from 2 million to 1 trillion, but most are around 11 million or fewer.
About 1.74 million species had been catalogued by 2018, and over 80% of species have not yet been described.
Biodiversity rises with the formation of new species and falls with extinction; the background rate is about one extinction per million species-years.
Insects dominate described species, with about 1,000,000 described and an estimated 5,000,000 in all.
Habitat destruction, often to expand farming, is currently a bigger driver of biodiversity loss than climate change.
Of the 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets set in 2010, only six were 'partially achieved' by 2020.

contested_note: Estimates of the total number of species differ enormously, and some, such as a trillion species, are disputed.

definition.text: Biodiversity trend indicators are indices that track how the world's biodiversity is changing over time.

facts.text: The Living Planet Index combines population data for many vertebrate species into one number; the 2012 global index showed a 28% decrease.
The Red List Index tracks changes in the IUCN conservation status of fully assessed groups such as mammals, birds, amphibians and corals.
No single indicator covers all species, and gaps in data and in time coverage limit them.

definition.text: Habitat conservation is the management of habitats to protect and restore them and to stop species from going extinct, being fragmented or losing range.

facts.text: Natural habitats provide ecosystem services, such as timber from forests and clean water from streams.
Conserving habitat can pay through tourism and outdoor recreation, and repairing damaged ecosystems is thought to cost far more than conserving them.
Putting a value on conserving different areas is often criticised as too utilitarian.
Biodiversity hotspots and the homes of flagship, umbrella or endangered species usually get priority.
Wild relatives of crops resist disease better; the wild corn teosinte resists 4 corn diseases, so seed banks plus habitat conservation are proposed for food security.
Adaptive management handles scientific uncertainty by gathering information and adjusting conservation plans over time.
Conservation principles were first applied in practice to the forests of British India in the 18th and 19th centuries.

definition.text: Habitat restoration is the part of habitat conservation that helps a degraded, damaged or destroyed ecosystem recover.

facts.text: It involves a plan with set goals, followed by monitoring and evaluating the species involved.
Restoring habitats altered by people has become a global effort to counter habitat destruction.
Miller and Hobbs name three kinds of constraint on restoration: ecological, economic and social.

title: Classes of environmental value

definition.text: Pearce and Moran sorted the values of the environment into direct extractive uses, indirect uses, option uses, bequest value and passive use value.

facts.text: Direct extractive uses include timber and food; indirect uses are ecosystem services such as flood control, pest control and erosion protection.
Option uses are possible future uses, such as unknown medicines from plants.
Bequest value is the benefit of knowing others may benefit in future; passive use value is enjoyment of a species' mere existence.

notes: Likely duplicates a total economic value entry in an economics chapter; fold at merge if so.

definition.text: Human impact on the environment means the changes people cause, directly or indirectly, to physical environments, ecosystems, biodiversity and natural resources.

facts.text: Reshaping the environment for society is causing global warming, ocean acidification, mass extinction, biodiversity loss and ecological collapse.
Global-scale damage is linked to population growth, rapid economic growth, overconsumption, overexploitation, pollution and deforestation.
Impacts grew sharply after the Industrial Revolution of the 1700s, but people have changed their surroundings since they first spread across the Earth.
A 2018 study found 87% of the oceans and 77% of land outside Antarctica altered by people, with 23% of the land left as wilderness.
Global Footprint Network estimates put humanity's demand 70% above what all the planet's ecosystems can regenerate.
Domesticated cattle and pigs outweigh all wild mammals by 14 to 1, and the world's chickens weigh three times as much as all wild birds.
The 2019 IPBES report names overfishing as the main driver of mass species extinction in the oceans.

title: Indirect drivers of environmental change
article: Human impact on the environment#Indirect drivers

definition.text: Indirect drivers are the political, economic and social forces that give rise to the human activities that harm the environment.

facts.text: They include population, economic development, urbanization, technology and climate change.
They differ from direct drivers, such as mining, agriculture, urban infrastructure and transport, which result from them.
Overconsumption, resource use beyond what ecosystems can sustain, can be measured with the ecological footprint.
Impact depends on lifestyle, affluence and pollution as much as on the raw number of people.
Cultural values matter too: how a society views nature shapes how much effort it makes to preserve it.

contested_note: Blaming population growth for environmental problems is controversial, and critics say it can unduly blame poor people in the Global South.

definition.text: In-situ conservation protects species and their genetic resources on site, in the natural populations where they live.

facts.text: Its opposite is ex situ conservation, where threatened species or their material are kept elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks.
Methods include nature reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biodiversity hotspots and gene sanctuaries.
It keeps populations in the setting where they developed their traits and lets evolution and adaptation carry on.
Reserves must be large enough to hold populations with the genetic diversity needed to keep adapting.
Ex situ conservation is a last resort when in situ conservation is too difficult or impossible.

definition.text: A biosphere reserve is a protected area designed to serve both biodiversity conservation and sustainable development.

facts.text: The concept dates from the 1970s and uses core, buffer and transition zones to balance conservation with development.
By 2004 about 459 such areas had been set up in 97 countries.
A gene sanctuary, where plants are conserved, includes both biosphere reserves and national parks.

definition.text: On-farm conservation keeps traditional crop varieties alive by improving them with farmers in their own fields.

facts.text: Gene-bank samples and farmers' seed of a variety are tested together, the best are crossed and multiplied, and the improved seed goes back to producers.
This lets farmers keep their own varieties instead of switching to commercial ones or abandoning the crop.
It works best in marginal areas where climate or soil rule out commercial varieties, or where taste makes up for lower yields.

title: Insular biogeography

definition.text: Island biogeography studies what controls the number and diversification of species in isolated natural communities.

facts.text: Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson started the field in the 1960s.
Its theory holds that an island's species number is set by a balance between immigration and extinction.
Remote islands receive fewer immigrants, while larger islands have more habitat and lower chance-driven extinction.
An 'island' can be any patch of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable land, such as a mountaintop, a woodland or a national park amid development.
Simberloff and Wilson cleared arthropods from small Florida mangrove islands; within a year they were recolonized, nearer islands fastest.
Seeing reserves as habitat islands raised fears they would lose species, and led to the SLOSS debate and to wildlife corridors.

contested_note: Ecologists vigorously debated its use in reserve design, notably whether one large reserve beats several small ones.

definition.text: Key Biodiversity Areas are places judged internationally important for biodiversity under global criteria published by the IUCN.

facts.text: They identify areas that governments or other agencies need to protect, extending the Important Bird Area idea to other groups.
Sites qualify on vulnerability and irreplaceability; the global standard was published in 2016.
The standard covers over 16,000 areas totalling 21,000,000 km2.
