Critics say the criteria may be too broad: one analysis found 26% to 68% of Earth's land could qualify.

definition.text: Biodiversity is measured with objective indicators, most often the number of taxa found in an area over a period of time.

facts.text: Species richness, species evenness and species diversity are worked out first; diversity combines richness and evenness.
The Shannon and Simpson diversity indices are the two most popular measures.
Diversity can be measured at different scales: alpha within a site, beta between sites and gamma across a region.
Each measure suits a particular use of the data; a more economically defensible one would preserve options for adaptation and future human use.
Since it is unclear which genes may prove useful, keeping as many genes as possible is the best choice for conservation.

definition.text: The Biodiversity Intactness Index measures change in biodiversity using worldwide abundance data on plants, fungi and animals.

facts.text: It shows how local land biodiversity responds to pressures such as land-use change and intensification.
The related Mean Species Abundance Index tracks population trends across a cross-section of species.
Northern Africa, southern Australia, coastal Brazil, Madagascar and South Africa show striking losses in biodiversity intactness.

title: Phylogenetic and functional diversity
article: Measurement of biodiversity#Other measures of diversity

definition.text: Phylogenetic and functional diversity measures add information on how species are related and on their functional traits, not just their number.

facts.text: Examples include Faith's 1992 phylogenetic diversity index and functional group richness.
Different kinds of diversity are not necessarily independent; vertebrate taxonomic and ecological diversity are closely linked.

definition.text: Nature conservation is the ethic and movement devoted to saving species from extinction, keeping and restoring habitats, enhancing ecosystem services and protecting biodiversity.

facts.text: Its goals include conserving habitat, preventing deforestation, keeping soil organic matter, halting extinctions, reducing overfishing and mitigating climate change.
As of 2018, 15% of land and 7.3% of the oceans were protected, and many environmentalists aim to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
Protected areas in developing countries, home to perhaps 70–80% of the world's species, still get very little effective management.
Private fundraising is not enough to pay for managing the more than 10% of the world that is legally protected.
Gifford Pinchot coined the term 'conservation' in 1907.
Early national parks often protected 'worthless lands' of little commercial interest, such as alpine and dry habitats.

definition.text: Conservation rests on different values, from nature's intrinsic worth to its usefulness for human wellbeing.

facts.text: Biocentrism gives intrinsic value to individual organisms, while ecoholism values whole species or ecosystems.
Utilitarian, anthropocentric conservation seeks a proper valuation of human impacts on nature in terms of human wellbeing now and in future.
How these values are assessed and traded among people shapes the social and political limits on conservation.
Some branches, such as compassionate conservation, focus on the welfare of sentient animals.

definition.text: Conservation seeks the proper use of nature, while preservation seeks to protect nature from use.

facts.text: In the early-20th-century environmental movement, conservationists wanted to regulate human use, while preservationists wanted to remove human impact altogether.
C. Anne Claus distinguishes 'conservation-far', which protects nature by separating it from people, from 'conservation-near'.

definition.text: Evidence-based conservation means basing conservation decisions and policy on systematically assessed evidence.

facts.text: Evidence includes peer-reviewed science, practitioners' experience, expert assessment and local and Indigenous knowledge, along with economic factors.
It arose because decisions relying on intuition and experience had led to costly, poor outcomes.
It borrows from evidence-based practice in medicine.

title: Poaching

definition.text: Poaching is the illegal hunting or capture of wild animals, and since the 1980s also the illegal harvesting of wild plants.

facts.text: It harms biodiversity inside and outside protected areas by depleting species and disturbing how ecosystems function.
In rural Africa the main motives are lack of jobs and limited farming potential; bushmeat sales bring cash income from cities.
International markets draw organised gangs, with crime syndicates trafficking body parts abroad.
Removing large animals defaunates forests, shifting seed dispersal so large-seeded trees dominate and small-seeded plants vanish locally.
Poachers treat the edges of protected areas as open-access resources, shrinking their effective size, and wildlife tourism loses income.
As many as 35,000 African elephants are killed each year for ivory.
Sustainable Development Goal 15 calls for action against the poaching and trafficking of protected species.

contested_note: Critics argue the label 'poaching' has been used to criminalise Indigenous peoples' traditional subsistence hunting.

definition.text: Anti-poaching efforts can target the supply of poached goods or the demand for them, and the economics of each differ.

facts.text: Supply-side remedies include stronger laws and enforcement and giving local communities land rights so they protect wildlife.
Through the snob effect, cutting supply makes goods rarer and pricier, which can draw wealthy buyers and offset enforcement gains.
Some evidence suggests reducing consumer demand works better than ever-more policing, though few demand campaigns evaluate their impact.
Listing rhinos on CITES Appendix I raised the price of horn and fuelled more poaching, but rhinos survived where on-the-ground protection was adequate.

definition.text: Soil biodiversity is the variety of life in soil and the soil properties that can be managed to support it.

facts.text: Soil is habitat mainly for microbes such as bacteria and fungi, but also for protozoa, nematodes, microarthropods, earthworms, termites and millipedes.
Soil organisms' main role is recycling organic matter from the plant-based food web above ground.
Keeping soil fertile is called one of the most vital ecological services the living world performs.
Microbial secretions dominate the binding of soil particles into aggregates and protect soil carbon from breakdown.
Erosion, acidification, salinisation and chloride from potash fertilizer all threaten soil organisms.
Because soils are a dispersed asset, soil health is best secured by a broad, consistent and economically appealing approach, such as liming or no-till farming.
A football pitch is estimated to hold underground organisms equal in mass to 500 sheep.

definition.text: Species diversity is the number of different species represented in a community, often weighted by how evenly individuals are spread among them.

facts.text: It can mean species richness, taxonomic or phylogenetic diversity, or species evenness.
It is often expressed as the effective number of species: how many equally abundant species would give the same average abundance as the data.
Researchers often quantify it with indices such as species richness, the Shannon index and the Simpson index, whose values are not directly comparable.
A sample usually underestimates the diversity of the whole population, so sampling effort must be standardised before comparisons.
Sampling a larger area raises observed diversity, because it includes more individuals and more varied environments.

definition.text: Diversity of order q is a family of diversity measures, the inverse of a weighted generalized mean of species' proportional abundances.

facts.text: At q = 0 it equals species richness; as q approaches 1 it becomes the exponential of Shannon entropy.
Raising q gives more weight to the most abundant species, so larger q yields lower diversity for the same data.
If all species are equally abundant, every value of q gives the species richness.

definition.text: Species evenness describes how equal the abundances of the species in a community are, that is, how common or rare each one is.

facts.text: Combined with species richness, it determines species diversity, a key measure of community structure.
Two meadows with four butterfly species each have equal richness, but the one split 25% each is more diverse than one where a single species makes up 80%.
Abundances are estimated by area-based counts, distance methods or mark-and-recapture studies.

title: Species richness

definition.text: Species richness is simply the number of different species in a community, landscape or region.

facts.text: It ignores how abundant each species is, so it is not the same as species diversity, which also accounts for evenness.
Larger samples tend to contain more species, so richness values are comparable only when sampling effort is standardised.
Many groups of organisms have the most species in the tropics, creating latitudinal gradients in richness.
It is often used to judge the conservation value of habitats, but it is blind to species identity: areas with many endemic or rare species usually count for more.

contested_note: Studies of how productivity relates to species richness disagree, and no global consensus has emerged.

definition.text: A threatened species is any animal, plant or fungus species vulnerable to extinction in the near future.

facts.text: The IUCN, the foremost authority, groups three categories as threatened: critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable.
Near threatened, least concern, not evaluated and data deficient species are not counted as threatened.
Threatened species are also called red-listed species, after the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species.
About 40% of the 40,177 species assessed under IUCN Red List criteria are listed as threatened, a total of 16,119.
Subspecies, populations and stocks can also be classed as threatened.

definition.text: A wildlife corridor is an area that links wildlife populations cut off from each other by farms, cities, roads and other development.

facts.text: Corridors reduce the harm of habitat fragmentation, a major threat to biodiversity.
Letting animals move between populations prevents the inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity seen in isolated groups, and spreads pollen and seeds.
By linking warmer and cooler habitat, corridors help species shift their ranges as the climate changes.
They can be continuous strips of habitat or 'stepping stones' of small separate patches, and include river zones and road crossings.
In a South Carolina experiment, butterflies were two to four times more likely to move to a patch linked by a corridor than to unlinked patches.
Success needs a shared vision among stakeholders, clear rules and incentive programmes to bring in private landowners.
Corridors can overlap with settlements and bring human–wildlife conflict such as crop raiding and livestock predation.

definition.text: Wildlife crossings are overpasses and underpasses that let animals cross roads, canals and other infrastructure safely.

facts.text: Species differ in which they prefer; in Banff National Park, black bears and mountain lions favour the darker underpasses.
Banff's network of six overpasses and 38 underpasses along the Trans-Canada Highway has cut wildlife collisions by 80%.
Fencing often complements crossings to reduce road deaths.

definition.text: Wildlife trade is the exchange of products from wild animals or plants, taken from nature or raised in captivity, whether alive, dead or as parts.

facts.text: Legal trade is regulated by CITES, which has 184 member countries, called Parties.
Global imports of wildlife products were worth US$187 billion in 2012, of which fisheries made up $113 billion.
Illegal wildlife trade is one of the major illegal economic activities, comparable to drug and arms trafficking; Interpol puts it at $10 billion to $20 billion a year.
Trade and other use are the second major threat to endangered mammals and among the top ten threats to birds, amphibians and cycads.
Live wildlife markets have been linked to outbreaks of zoonotic diseases including COVID-19, H5N1 bird flu, SARS and mpox.
Customs codes record most wildlife imports only under broad categories, so the trade is poorly monitored.
Legal trade with quotas, as for Florida alligators, can give an economic incentive to keep habitat.

title: Legalizing trade in endangered species
article: Wildlife trade#Legalising trade for endangered species

definition.text: Whether to allow legal trade in products from endangered species is a highly controversial question.

facts.text: Supporters say a regulated market could push down prices of illegal goods, cutting the incentive to poach, or raise money for conservation.
Laundering and corruption are major obstacles, as illegal goods get passed off as legal.
CITES bans commercial trade in wild Appendix I species, while Appendix II and III trade is allowed if it is shown not to harm wild populations.

contested_note: Researchers disagree over whether legal markets help endangered species or open the door to laundering of illegal goods.

definition.text: Forest genetic resources are the genetic material, of present or future value, of forest tree and shrub species.

facts.text: Forest communities depend on them for timber and non-timber products such as fruits, gums and resins, and they underpin plantation wood production.
The FAO's first State of the World's Forest Genetic Resources in 2014 found half the regularly used forest species threatened by land conversion, overexploitation and climate change.
Their diversity lets tree species adapt to climate change, but not all can adapt fast enough, so moving forest reproductive material may be needed.

definition.text: Climate change is altering how widely and heavily many infectious diseases are transmitted around the world.

facts.text: Warmer, wetter conditions let vectors such as mosquitoes and ticks survive in places once too cold or dry, so dengue and Lyme disease now appear at higher latitudes and elevations.
Warmer water and more flooding spread bacteria such as Vibrio cholerae, while drought and poor water access raise the risk of diarrheal diseases.
Deforestation, habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss add to zoonotic risk, as people encroach on habitats and ecosystems favour efficient disease reservoirs.
Low-income communities with weak healthcare and sanitation are the most vulnerable, and diseases like malaria slow their path to prosperity, worsening global inequality.
The UN Environment Programme says the most fundamental protection against zoonotic diseases is to prevent the destruction of nature.
Responses increasingly follow the One Health approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health as one.
